summary: Evaluates existing GMPLS routing and signaling protocols against the Optical Channel Data Unit containers introduced in ITU-T G.709-2012. It is informational and looks at what changes might be needed.

plainLanguage.summary: Optical transport networks pack small signals into bigger ones in containers of fixed size. GMPLS routing and signalling were written for the older version of that standard and cannot yet describe the newer containers, the finer slot size or the way signals are stacked. This RFC lists what is missing.

subtitle: Which parts of the new optical transport containers the GMPLS routing and signalling protocols cannot yet express.

tldr.problem: GMPLS routing and signalling were built for the 2001 edition of the ITU-T G.709 optical transport specification. The 2012 edition adds containers, multiplexing relationships and a finer tributary slot size that those protocols cannot describe.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through the new optical structure and checks it against the protocols one feature at a time: tributary slot granularity and its payload type, the tributary port number, the signal type, bit rate and tolerance, unreserved resources, maximum LSP bandwidth, terminating against switching capability, priority, multi-stage multiplexing and the label format.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that defines no protocol elements. Its conclusion is that both routing and signalling need extensions to carry the new information, and the companion documents on OSPF and RSVP extensions address the gaps it identifies.

today: RFC 7096 is an Informational RFC published in January 2014. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the gap analysis between GMPLS and the 2012 edition of the G.709 optical transport specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
GMPLS routing, in OSPF and IS-IS, and GMPLS signalling, in RSVP-TE, provide the mechanisms for basic GMPLS control of Optical Transport Networks based on the 2001 revision of the G.709 specification. The 2012 revision of that specification includes new optical transport features that GMPLS does not support.

This document evaluates the existing GMPLS signalling and routing protocols against the requirements of G.709. Background information and a framework for the GMPLS protocol extensions needed to support G.709 is provided in RFC 7062, and the specific routing and signalling extensions defined in the OTN-OSPF and OTN-RSVP documents address the gaps identified here.

The document's method is to take the traffic engineering information needed for path computation and the parameters needed to set up a label switched path, and to check each type of data against what GMPLS already carries and what it is missing.
sections.plainLanguage: The optical standards moved on in 2012 and the routing and signalling protocols did not follow. This RFC goes through the new features one by one and lists what each protocol cannot yet say.

sections.title: The Optical Structure
sections.content:
The digital optical transport structure has two layers. The digital path layer is the ODU, the Optical channel Data Unit, and the digital section layer is the OTU, the Optical channel Transport Unit. An OTU section layer supports one ODU path layer as a client and provides monitoring for the optical channel that carries the digital structure. An ODU path layer may transport a heterogeneous assembly of ODU clients, and the fixed-size containers ODU1, ODU2, ODU3 and ODU4 may each act as a client or a server depending on the networking domain. The flexible container ODUflex is the exception, because it carries whatever bit rate it is given.

The tables below come from the G.872 recommendation and set out which client a given server will accept. The fixed containers grow in steps: ODU1 sits in an OTU 1 and takes a 2.5 Gbit/s client or an ODU0; ODU2 sits in an OTU 2 and takes a 10 Gbit/s client, an ODU0, an ODU1 or an ODUflex; ODU3 sits in an OTU 3 and takes a 40 Gbit/s client down to ODU0; ODU4 sits in an OTU 4 and takes a 100 Gbit/s client down to ODU0. ODUflex is different: it takes constant bit rate clients from just above 2.5 Gbit/s up to 100 Gbit/s, or Generic Framing Procedure framed packet clients from 1.25 Gbit/s up to 100 Gbit/s.

In a multiplexing scenario the lower order signal is called ODUj and the higher order one ODUk. How an ODUk connection service is carried inside an operator's network is a matter of policy: the service may be transported over an ODUk path inside an OTUk section, consuming a whole wavelength of capacity, or the operator may multiplex ODUk signals before transport over rate ODU servers so that the network is used more efficiently. The same ODUk can play different roles as it crosses different domains, and client ODUk services may be carried over wavelength subnetworks, over ODU links with sub-lambda or lambda granularity, or over a mix of the two.
sections.plainLanguage: The optical network has fixed-size containers that carry smaller containers inside them, and one flexible container that carries whatever bit rate it is given. A provider chooses whether to fill a whole wavelength or to pack smaller signals into it.

sections.title: Tributary Slot Granularity
sections.content:
G.709 defines two tributary slot granularities, and the granularity is chosen per layer, so both ends of a link may pick different ones. If both ends run new cards that support both the 1.25 Gbit/s and the 2.5 Gbit/s granularities, the link works with 1.25 Gbit/s slots. If one end supports both and the other is an old card that supports only 2.5 Gbit/s slots, the link works with 2.5 Gbit/s slots.

On the data plane, an ODUk container is an Optical channel Payload Unit plus its overhead. Inside the payload unit overhead sits the payload structure identifier, which carries the payload type telling the composition of the signal. When an ODUj signal is multiplexed into an ODUk it is extended with frame alignment overhead and mapped into an Optical channel Data Tributary Unit. Two kinds exist: the ODTUjk containers, where the lower order signal is mapped by the Asynchronous Mapping Procedure, and the ODTUk.ts containers with ts slots, mapped by the Generic Mapping Procedure. A payload type of 0x20 means the structure holds only ODTUjk units, and 0x21 means it holds ODTUk.ts units or both. The distinction is needed for OPU2 and OPU3, which can carry either structure; OPU4 only supports 0x21 and OPU1 only 0x20. The relationship with granularity is that the 0x20 structure has 2.5 Gbit/s slots and the 0x21 structure has 1.25 Gbit/s slots.

When the AUTOpayloadtype is configured, a node compares the payload type it received with the one it transmits and, if they differ and it transmits 0x21, it falls back to 0x20. The fallback makes the system self-consistent, and the only reason left to signal the granularity is to give the right label, since the label for 0x21 has twice as many slot numbers as the label for 0x20. When AUTOpayloadtype is not configured, the RSVP-TE consequent actions for a slot mismatch have to be defined.

On the control plane there are two granularities to keep apart. The server granularity is what maps an end-to-end ODUj onto a server ODUk path or link, and the ODUj cannot influence it; the ODUj is simply mapped onto whatever slots are available. The client granularity is one of the parameters needed to pick the adaptation towards the client layers at the end nodes, and it is the only thing the ODUj has to guarantee. The example in the RFC makes the point that granularity processing is a per-layer issue: an ODU3 path created with a 2.5 Gbit/s client granularity can still carry an ODU2 path that promises a 1.25 Gbit/s client granularity. In a multi-stage hierarchy such as ODU0 to ODU2 to ODU3, each level can have a different granularity, so every level has to advertise its capabilities for the path computation to be correct.
sections.plainLanguage: Optical links can cut their capacity into 1.25 or 2.5 Gbit/s slots. The router has to know which sizes each hop supports before it can pick a path, and the signalling has to carry that choice along.

sections.title: Tributary Port Number and Bit Rate
sections.content:
The signalling extensions for optical transport, RFC 4328, support only the deprecated auto-MSI mode, in which the Tributary Port Number is assigned automatically in the transmit direction and not checked in the receive direction. In G.709 and G.798 the payload unit overhead of an OTUk frame carries one MSI byte per tributary slot of the ODUk, in multiframe form, each indicating the association between a tributary port number and a slot. That association has to be configured by the control plane and checked by the data plane on each side of the link, so RSVP-TE signalling needs an extension to carry out the port number assignment.

Bit rate and tolerance are another area. In the current traffic parameters signalling both are implied by the signal type. ODUflex in constant bit rate mode and ODUflex in packet mode can have variable bit rates, so the traffic parameters have to be upgraded. Tolerance needs no change, because a fixed value is defined for each signal type: plus or minus 100 parts per million, or plus or minus 20 parts per million depending on the signal type.
sections.plainLanguage: Each slot in a container has to be matched to a port number on the far side, and the two ends have to agree on that. The signalling cannot currently carry the assignment, and it also cannot carry a variable bit rate.

sections.title: What the Routing Protocols Cannot Say Yet
sections.content:
Signal type. From a routing point of view, GMPLS OSPF and IS-IS can only advertise interfaces with a single tributary slot type and no precise information about how bandwidth is allocated. With link bundling, dividing the unreserved bandwidth by the maximum LSP bandwidth does not reveal how many maximum-size LSPs actually fit. The lack of spatial allocation information hits the restoration process hard, because not knowing which resources are free greatly increases the number of crankbacks and so the convergence time. The tools available also allow either fixed bandwidth with implicit hierarchy, as in SDH and SONET, or variable bandwidth with no hierarchy, as in packet switching, but not a mixture such as ODUflex constant bit rate alongside ODUflex packet. One way out would be a separate Interface Switching Capability Descriptor for every signal type the link supports, but the RFC notes that this multiplies the number of descriptors, and that OSPF and IS-IS messages have size limits because IP fragmentation is to be avoided and IS-IS does not support messages larger than a link's frame.

Unreserved resources. These have to be advertised per priority and per signal type for restoration to work. RFC 4203 allows advertising them per priority only, which leaves uncertainty about how many LSPs of a given signal type can be restored. The RFC's example is a traffic engineering link made of three ODU3 component links with 32, 24 and 24 slots, supporting ODU2 and ODU3 signal types, advertised as 80 slots of unreserved bandwidth and a maximum LSP bandwidth of 32 slots. During restoration the network could try to restore two ODU3s, 64 slots, when only one can fit, and a crankback follows.

Terminating and switching capabilities. An interface's capability needs to distinguish the two, because an internal constraint may let a signal be only switched, that is forwarded to the switching matrix without multiplexing or demultiplexing, or only terminated, that is demultiplexed, or both. In the RFC's example the interface can multiplex an ODU2 coming from the switching matrix into an ODU3 and map it into an OTU3, and can map an ODU3 from the matrix into an OTU3, so the advertised bandwidth is ODU2 with switching capability and ODU3 with both. Without this, a path computation can pick a link that cannot actually carry the traffic: in one example the restore of an ODU2 path has to avoid an OTU3 link because the far node can only extract the service from an OTU2 link. The RFC notes that the problem is general rather than specific to optical transport.

Multi-stage multiplexing, priority and the label format. Multi-stage multiplexing needs the advertisement of cascaded adaptation capabilities together with the matrix access constraints, using the Interface Adaptation Capability Descriptor. In a hierarchy such as ODU1 to ODU2 to ODU3, the intermediate bandwidth is needed as well as the top and the bottom one, because the spatial allocation decides whether the middle container can be built at all: a spread of 3 plus 2 leaves no room for an ODU2, while 4 plus 1 leaves room for one. Priority is less urgent, since the inefficiency in advertising every priority does not stop optical transport from working. Finally, the label format for ODUk defined in RFC 4328 could be extended for the new signal types but would be hard to extend again later, and it has scalability problems: an ODU3 mapped into an ODU4 with 1.25 Gbit/s slots needs 31 labels, which is 992 bits, and an ODUflex into an ODU4 may need up to 80 labels, which is 2560 bits. A new flexible and scalable label format is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The routing protocols cannot say which containers a link really supports, how the capacity is spread across bundled links, or whether an interface can end a signal or only pass it along. Each of those gaps makes path computation guess, and guessing produces failed paths and slow restoration.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document defines new types of information to be carried that describe optical transport containers and hierarchies, but it defines no new protocol elements. From a security point of view it therefore introduces no further risks with respect to the information that GMPLS protocols can already convey. For a general discussion of MPLS and GMPLS security issues the RFC points to the MPLS and GMPLS security framework, RFC 5920.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no protocol elements of its own, so it adds no new security exposure. The general MPLS and GMPLS security rules still apply.

viz.caption: THE PIECES OF THE TRIBUTARY SLOT PROBLEM

items.title: Two slot sizes
items.text: A link can cut its capacity into 1.25 Gbit/s or 2.5 Gbit/s slots, and the choice is per layer.

items.title: Payload type 0x20
items.text: The container holds only ODTUjk units, mapped by the asynchronous mapping procedure.

items.title: Payload type 0x21
items.text: The container holds ODTUk.ts units, or both kinds, mapped by the generic mapping procedure.

items.title: Server granularity
items.text: What maps the end-to-end ODUj onto the server container. The ODUj cannot influence it.

items.title: Client granularity
items.text: What the ODUj promises to the client layer. It is the only thing the ODUj has to guarantee.

items.title: Fallback
items.text: A node that transmits 0x21 and receives 0x20 falls back to 0x20, so the two ends stay consistent.

viz.caption: THE GAPS BETWEEN GMPLS AND THE NEW OPTICAL CONTAINERS

cells: Advertises interfaces with a single slot type and no spatial allocation detail
A way to advertise each container the link supports
Advertisement per priority and per signal type
A separate capability for each, advertised with the bandwidth
Only the top and bottom layers are described
The intermediate layer and the spatial allocation
One label per slot, fixed format
A flexible format that scales to large paths
